endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Relevant testing may include multi-turn simulated encounters that assess time to escalation in evolving presentations, the quality of escalation language and handoff information, and resistance to over-reassurance when users minimize symptoms or resist escalation.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether evaluating AI escalation messages for clarity, actionability, empathy, and comprehension across health literacy levels leads users to understand or act on escalation advice. The recommendation currently rests on one regulatory discussion paper that describes such testing as something evaluators may include.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains no studies that test the practice and no studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a discussion paper, and it expresses the practice with the permissive term "may," which places it at the level of expert suggestion.

The one endorsing source is a regulatory discussion paper on generative AI medical devices. It lists the quality of escalation language, handoff information, and resistance to over-reassurance as possible test targets in multi-turn simulated encounters. The paper frames these as considerations, and it does not establish a requirement or a pass threshold for comprehension across literacy levels.

The recommendation names comprehension across health literacy levels, yet no supplied study measures escalation message comprehension in low-literacy, limited English proficiency, Medicaid, or safety-net users. Without such data, a health system cannot tell whether escalation language that tests well in general samples will be understood by the patients most likely to face barriers to acting on it.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare escalation messages evaluated for clarity, actionability, and empathy against unevaluated messages, and that measure user comprehension, time to escalation, and whether users seek the recommended care. These studies should stratify results by health literacy and language, and should first document how often escalation advice from AI tools is misunderstood or ignored.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of this practice was supplied, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The recommendation's reference to health literacy levels therefore reflects intent, and health systems serving these populations have no data on whether such evaluation improves understanding for their patients.
